body.heading: Small enough to survive busy days
paragraphs: The after-dinner walk works because it is modest: around the block, to the end of the street and back, fifteen or twenty minutes. It does not need a destination, special clothes, or good weather every time, though a turnaround point helps on reluctant evenings.
Attach it to something that already happens. Plates cleared, shoes on. When the walk follows dinner automatically, nobody has to decide afresh each night whether they feel like it.

body.heading: Walking loosens conversation
paragraphs: People often talk more easily side by side than face to face. Children mention things on a walk that never came up at the table, and adults do too. There is no need to fill every silence; noticing the same dog, the same garden, the same moon is its own kind of conversation.
A simple game keeps younger walkers going: count cats, spot something red, listen for the furthest sound. Rotate a small route or two so the walk stays familiar without getting stale.

body.heading: Keep it weatherproof-ish
paragraphs: Rain shortens the walk rather than cancelling it, most days. Umbrellas and a loop of ten minutes still count. The habit matters more than the distance.

description: A short walk after dinner is one of the easiest family habits to start, because it asks for nothing but shoes and twenty minutes.
